pos: n. (Robert Browne, c. 1550–1633, first theorist of English Separatism, author of A Treatise of Reformation without Tarying for Anie)
etymology: English surname Browne, from the colour; Brownism was the name given to Separatism from him.
biblical_def: Robert Browne was a Cambridge man and a kinsman of Lord Burghley who in 1581 gathered a covenanted congregation at Norwich on the principle that a true church is a company of believers joined by mutual covenant under Christ, with power to choose and depose its own officers. Driven abroad, he printed at Middelburg in 1582 the tract that made him famous, A Treatise of Reformation without Tarying for Anie, which argued that the duty of reforming the church does not wait upon the permission of the magistrate or the bishops, because obedience to Christ is not suspended while the authorities deliberate. Two men were hanged at Bury St Edmunds in 1583 for distributing his books. Browne himself afterwards submitted to the Church of England and held a Northamptonshire living until his death, dying in Northampton gaol after striking a constable. Act 5:29 is the tract's whole argument, that “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a separatist as one that withdraws from an established church, and a covenant as a mutual consent or agreement.
webster_full: SEP'ARATIST, n. One that withdraws or separates himself from an established church, to which he has belonged; a dissenter.
COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
REFORMA'TION, n. The act of reforming; correction or amendment of life, manners, or of any thing vicious or corrupt.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Rev 18:4
And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.
corruption_summary: He wrote that reformation need not wait for permission, and then spent fifty years conforming.
corruption_paragraphs: Browne's argument has not been answered within the terms of an established church. If the duty of ordering worship by Christ's command is a duty, it is owed now, and a believer who defers it until the magistrate consents has made the magistrate the judge of his obedience. 2Co 6:17 commands separation from what is unclean — “come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — and Rev 18:4 repeats it as a summons out, not a petition to those within.

The man's own course is the hard part and the dictionary states it plainly rather than quietly. Having given English Separatism its founding argument and its nickname, Browne conformed, took a parish living from the church he had unchurched, and lived on it for forty years while the men who had believed him went to Amsterdam, to prison, and in two cases to the gallows. The dictionary honours the argument and does not honour the retreat. Mat 18:17 gives the congregation a real authority, and that principle outlived its author's courage.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; aphorizo (G873), to separate; ekklesia (G1577), assembly.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
Greek exerchomai (G1831) — to come out, go forth; 2 Corinthians 6:17.
Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, set apart; 2 Corinthians 6:17.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the tract in one sentence.
“come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — a summons, not a petition.
“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — the congregation's real authority.

pos: n. (John Greenwood, d. 1593, Separatist minister, hanged at Tyburn with Henry Barrow)
etymology: English surname Greenwood, a dweller by the green wood.
biblical_def: John Greenwood was a Cambridge graduate and an ordained minister of the Church of England who renounced his orders, joined the Separatist congregation in London, and became its teacher alongside Henry Barrow. He was arrested in 1586 at a private house in St Andrew's Hill while the congregation was meeting, and spent nearly all his remaining years in the Clink and the Fleet, where he and Barrow wrote and smuggled out the books that set out the Separatist case. Released briefly, he was rearrested in December 1592. He and Barrow were convicted of publishing seditious books, twice brought to the gallows and twice reprieved at the last moment, and hanged at Tyburn on 6 April 1593. He left a wife and a young son. Rev 2:10 is the promise he died on, “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death in defense of his faith, and a conventicle as an assembly for worship, in a bad sense.
webster_full: MAR'TYR, n. One who by his death bears witness to the truth of the gospel; one who suffers death in defense of any opinion, particularly in defense of the Christian faith.
CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; usually, an assembly for religious worship, applied in reproach to the meetings of dissenters.
REPRIEVE', n. A respite; a temporary suspension of the execution of a sentence of death.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Mat 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
corruption_summary: Twice brought to the gallows and reprieved, hanged on the third morning for printing books.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge on which Greenwood and Barrow died was publishing seditious books, and the books argued that a congregation of believers may order its worship by Christ's command without a bishop's licence. The Elizabethan state treated that as a political crime because the establishment and the crown were one fabric; the dictionary names the execution as a judicial murder for a theological conviction. Mat 5:11 pronounces blessing on those against whom men “shall say all manner of evil against you falsely” (Mat 5:11), and sedition was the false word used.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that English Separatism was bought at the price of lives and not of debating points. 2Ti 3:12 says plainly that all who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution, and the Separatists of the 1590s are the English instance. The double reprieve is worth dwelling on: Greenwood was prepared to die twice before he actually did, which is a form of endurance the word martyrdom usually conceals.
roots_summary: Greek stephanos (G4735), a crown; oneidizo (G3679), to revile; dioko (G1377), to persecute.
usage: “be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — Tyburn, 6 April 1593.
“shall say all manner of evil against you falsely” (Mat 5:11) — the word was sedition.
“all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12) — the English instance.

pos: n. (John Penry, 1563–1593, Welsh Separatist, pleader for a preaching ministry in Wales, hanged at St Thomas Watering)
etymology: Welsh ap Henry, son of Henry, contracted to Penry.
biblical_def: John Penry was a Breconshire Welshman educated at Cambridge and Oxford who in 1587 laid before Parliament An Exhortation unto the Governours and People of Wales and other treatises making one demand: that Wales be given a preaching ministry in its own tongue. He documented parishes where no sermon had been preached in living memory and incumbents who could not read Welsh, and he argued that a people cannot believe what has never been preached to them. He was imprisoned for it, became connected with the secret press that issued the Marprelate tracts, fled to Scotland, returned, joined the London Separatist congregation after Barrow and Greenwood were hanged, was arrested within weeks, and was hanged at St Thomas Watering in Southwark on 29 May 1593, aged thirty. Rom 10:14 is the question he put to Parliament, “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religious subjects, and an exhortation as the act of inciting to laudable deeds.
webster_full: PREACH'ER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one that inculcates any thing with earnestness.
EXHORTA'TION, n. The act or practice of exhorting; the act of inciting to laudable deeds; incitement to that which is good.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as, English is our vernacular language.
scriptures: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: He asked Parliament for Welsh preaching and was hanged at thirty for the company he kept while asking.
corruption_paragraphs: Penry's petitions are among the clearest statements anywhere of what a preaching ministry is for. He did not argue that Welsh preaching would be edifying or culturally appropriate; he argued that souls perish without it, and he produced the parish evidence. Rom 10:14 is the logic and 1Co 9:16 the preacher's compulsion, “woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel” (1Co 9:16). Isa 52:7 supplies the valuation of such feet upon the mountains.

The corruption he exposed is the holding of a cure of souls as a source of income without the discharge of its duty. Pluralism, non-residence, and the appointment of men who could not speak the language of their parishioners were not abuses at the edge of the Elizabethan church; in Wales they were the system. Mat 5:10 pronounces the blessing on those persecuted for righteousness' sake, and Penry's death at thirty, on evidence of association rather than of any act, is where the complaint ended.
roots_summary: Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim; anagke (G318), necessity; Hebrew basar (H1319), to bear tidings.
roots_lines: Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; Romans 10:14.
Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear or bring tidings; Isaiah 52:7.
usage: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — his question to Parliament.
“woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel” (1Co 9:16) — the compulsion he felt.
“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet” (Isa 52:7) — what Wales had been denied.

pos: n. (Francis Johnson, 1562–1618, pastor of the Separatist Ancient Church in Amsterdam)
etymology: English patronymic John-son, son of John; Francis, from Latin Franciscus, Frenchman.
biblical_def: Francis Johnson was a Cambridge fellow who, as a university officer, was ordered to seize and burn the Separatist books of Henry Barrow coming off a press in Middelburg. He kept two copies to see what the heresy was, read them, and was convinced. He joined the London Separatist congregation, became its pastor, was imprisoned for years, and in 1597 went with the remnant to Amsterdam, where the body became known as the Ancient Church. He pastored it for twenty years. His later career was marked by two quarrels: a long and public dispute with his brother George and with Henry Ainsworth over whether final authority in the congregation rests with the eldership or with the whole body, which split the church in 1610; and a severe exercise of discipline against his own father and brother. 1Co 1:10 is the text his history enforces, that there be “no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church, and eldership as the office of an elder.
webster_full: PAS'TOR, n. A shepherd; one that has the care of flocks and herds. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
ELD'ERSHIP, n. The office of an elder; presbytery; order of elders.
EXILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country; banishment; the person banished.
scriptures: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
corruption_summary: He was ordered to burn the books that converted him, and then divided the church they had gathered.
corruption_paragraphs: Johnson's conversion by the books he had been sent to destroy is a genuine providence and worth recording. His pastorate is a harder lesson. The question that split the Ancient Church in 1610 was a real one — whether the keys are exercised by the elders on the congregation's behalf or by the congregation itself — and it is the question Mat 18:17 bears on most directly, since the final step there is “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17).

The corruption to name is the use of discipline as an instrument of a party. Johnson excommunicated his own father and brother in the course of the dispute, and a community that had fled persecution spent its exile litigating against itself. 1Pe 5:3 forbids the temper, elders not “being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3), and Act 15:6 shows apostles and elders deliberating together rather than one party overruling. The dictionary holds congregational government with a plurality of elders and reads the Amsterdam split as a warning about what a persecuted and idle exile congregation will do to itself.
roots_summary: Greek schisma (G4978), division; katakurieuo (G2634), to lord over; kleros (G2819), heritage.
roots_lines: Greek katartizo (G2675) — to join together, perfect; 1 Corinthians 1:10.
Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to lord it over; 1 Peter 5:3.
usage: “that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — what the exile church forgot.
“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — the question that split it.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3) — the temper forbidden.

pos: n. (Henry Ainsworth, c. 1569–1622, teacher of the Ancient Church in Amsterdam, Hebraist and annotator)
etymology: English surname Ainsworth, from a Lancashire place name, Aegen's enclosure.
biblical_def: Henry Ainsworth left Cambridge for the Separatist cause, lived in Amsterdam at one time as a porter in a bookseller's cellar on ninepence a week, and became the teacher of the Ancient Church beside Francis Johnson. He was one of the finest Hebraists in Europe. His Annotations upon the Five Books of Moses, the Book of the Psalmes and the Song of Songs gives the Hebrew text's sense word by word with rabbinic and Targumic material weighed and judged, and his metrical Psalter was carried to Plymouth by the Pilgrims and used there for decades. He divided from Johnson in 1610 over the authority of the eldership and led out the party that held the congregation's own power. Isa 8:20 is the standard he applied to the Jewish commentators he read so closely, and Luk 24:27 the end he read the Pentateuch for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an annotation as a remark or note on a text, and a Targum as a Chaldee paraphrase of the Old Testament.
webster_full: ANNOTA'TION, n. A remark, note or commentary on some passage of a book, intended to illustrate its meaning.
TAR'GUM, n. A Chaldee version or paraphrase of the Old Testament.
PSALM'ODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Psa 96:3
Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.
corruption_summary: A porter on ninepence a week who wrote the best Hebrew annotations in England.
corruption_paragraphs: Ainsworth is the answer to the assumption that separation from an establishment means separation from learning. He read the rabbis, the Targums, and the Septuagint, judged them by the text, and produced annotations that scholars still consult, while living in poverty in a foreign city as a member of a hunted congregation. Isa 8:20 is the discipline that kept the apparatus in its place: “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20), applied to Jewish and Christian commentators alike.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing of exact philology with a confessional aim. He did not read the Pentateuch to reconstruct its sources but to find what Luk 24:27 says is there, “in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). His Psalter is the other half of the man: having established the sense, he put the Psalms into English metre so that a congregation of exiles could sing them, and a shipload of them did, in Plymouth, for two generations.
roots_summary: Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; Greek diermeneuo (G1329), to expound; orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight.
usage: “if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20) — applied to every commentator.
“in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — why he read Moses.
“Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3) — the Psalter he made to be sung.

pos: n. (the congregation of English Separatist exiles at Amsterdam, c. 1593–1640, so named as the oldest of the exiled churches)
etymology: Latin antianus, former, through Old French ancien; so called because it was the earliest of the exiled English churches.
biblical_def: The Ancient Church was the name given to the congregation of English Separatists who fled to Amsterdam from the London persecutions of the 1590s, the remnant of the body Henry Barrow and John Greenwood had taught before they were hanged. Francis Johnson was its pastor and Henry Ainsworth its teacher. It was the oldest of the English exile churches and so the model and the warning for those that followed: John Smyth's company from Gainsborough and John Robinson's from Scrooby both came to Amsterdam and both drew away from it. It published the True Confession of 1596, kept a covenanted membership with a strict discipline, and divided in 1610 over the authority of the eldership, after which it declined. Heb 13:14 states the condition of every such congregation, that “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ancient as that happened in former times, and a church as a congregation of Christians united under one form of government.
webster_full: A'NCIENT, a. Old; that happened or existed in former times, usually at a great distance of time.
CHURCH, n. A congregation of Christians united under one form of ecclesiastical government, in one creed, and using the same ritual and ceremonies.
EX'ILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country; banishment.
scriptures: For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: The oldest of the exile churches, model to the Pilgrims and a warning to them.
corruption_paragraphs: The Ancient Church matters out of proportion to its size because every later English congregational body passed through or past it. Smyth's people and Robinson's both examined it, learned from its order, and declined to join it; Robinson moved his company to Leiden partly to get his flock away from its quarrels. Act 2:42 describes what such a congregation is supposed to continue in — “the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42) — and fellowship is the item the Ancient Church lost first.

The lesson the dictionary draws is about the conditions of exile rather than about the men. A congregation driven out of its country, deprived of its ordinary labour, concentrated in one quarter of a foreign city, and left with nothing to administer but itself will turn its energy inward. Heb 11:38 honours those of whom “the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) and Act 8:4 shows the scattered preaching wherever they went; the Amsterdam exiles did some of both, and also spent twenty years at law with each other.
roots_summary: Greek meno (G3306), to continue, abide; proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly; koinonia (G2842), fellowship.
usage: “here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) — the exile's condition.
“the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — fellowship was lost first.
“Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — true of them, and not the whole story.

pos: n. (the confession of faith published by the English Separatist exiles at Amsterdam in 1596, ancestor of the London Baptist Confession of 1644)
etymology: English true + Latin confessio, an acknowledgement; its running title was A True Confession of the Faith.
biblical_def: The True Confession of 1596 was published by the exiled Separatist congregation at Amsterdam under the title A True Confession of the Faith, and Humble Acknowledgment of the Alegeance, which wee hir Maiesties Subjects... doe hould. Its forty-five articles state the Reformed doctrines of God, Scripture, the fall, election, and justification in terms the English Puritans would have granted, and then set out the Separatist ecclesiology: that a visible church is a company of believers joined by covenant, that Christ has given it officers of its own choosing, that its discipline is exercised by the body, and that the worship and government of the church are to be ordered by the written word alone. It also professed loyal subjection to the queen in civil things. Its structure and much of its language passed into the First London Baptist Confession of 1644. Tit 1:9 names what a confession is for, holding fast the faithful word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as the acknowledgment of a creed or profession of faith, and allegiance as the tie which binds the subject to the sovereign.
webster_full: CONFES'SION, n. Avowal; the acknowledgment of a crime or fault; also, a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed to be assented to.
ALLE'GIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; the duty of fidelity to a king, government or state.
AR'TICLE, n. A single clause or item of an account or writing; a particular part of a creed or confession.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
corruption_summary: Forty-five articles from a hunted congregation, and the grandfather of the Baptist confessions.
corruption_paragraphs: The document is worth reading for what it refutes about Separatism. The common charge was that these men were enthusiasts who had left the church for a private spirit; the confession answers by stating, in order and in detail, the catholic and Reformed doctrines they held in common with those who were imprisoning them, and then identifying the precise points of difference as matters of ecclesiology governed by Scripture. Jud 1:3 is the warrant for publishing it, to “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lineage. The 1596 confession shaped the First London Baptist Confession of 1644, which was revised in 1646 and lies behind the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689 that the dictionary holds as its subordinate standard. 1Ti 3:15 names the church the pillar and ground of the truth, and a confession is how a congregation nails its colours where the next generation can read them. Heb 10:23 supplies the duty of holding the profession without wavering once it is made.
roots_summary: Greek homologia (G3671), profession, confession; hapax (G530), once for all; antechomai (G472), to hold fast.
roots_lines: Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; Jude 3.
usage: “Holding fast the faithful word” (Tit 1:9) — what a confession is for.
“earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — the warrant to print.
“hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23) — once made, kept.

pos: n. (the Lincolnshire town on the Trent where John Smyth's Separatist congregation gathered, c. 1606)
etymology: Old English Gegnes burh, the stronghold of Gegn; a market town on the river Trent.
biblical_def: Gainsborough is the Lincolnshire town where, about 1606, a Separatist congregation gathered under John Smyth, meeting largely in the great hall of the manor house with the connivance of its owner. It was one of two neighbouring companies that came out of the Church of England in those years; the other met at Scrooby under Richard Clyfton and John Robinson. Both covenanted together to walk in all the ways God had made known or should make known to them, and both were driven to Amsterdam by 1608. The Gainsborough company became, in exile, the first English Baptist church: Smyth concluded that a church gathered on a confession of faith must be baptized on that confession, and baptized himself and then his congregation in 1609. Thomas Helwys led a portion of it back to London in 1612. Act 2:42 describes what they covenanted to continue in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual agreement, and to gather as to bring together, to assemble.
webster_full: COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract.
GATH'ER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things; to assemble; to muster.
BAP'TISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
corruption_summary: A congregation in a manor hall on the Trent that became, in exile, the first English Baptist church.
corruption_paragraphs: The Gainsborough covenant is the beginning of a line that the dictionary stands in. The company bound itself to walk in all the ways of God already made known and still to be made known, which is a dangerous and necessary undertaking: it commits a congregation in advance to obey light it does not yet have. In Amsterdam the light they received was about baptism, and Smyth followed it where it led. 2Co 6:17 had already taken them out of the parish church; the same principle took them to the water.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the two steps. They did not first conclude that infant baptism was invalid and then separate; they first concluded that a church is a covenanted company of professing believers, and the baptismal question followed from that as a consequence. Mat 18:17 and Act 2:42 presume a bounded membership that can be told something and can continue in it. Heb 13:13 is what it cost: the manor hall, then Amsterdam, then for Helwys's party Newgate.
roots_summary: Greek proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly; aphorizo (G873), to separate; parembole (G3925), a camp.
usage: “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” (Act 2:42) — what they covenanted.
“come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — the first step.
“unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13) — and what it cost.

pos: n. (John Murton, c. 1585–1626, Gainsborough furrier, successor to Thomas Helwys as leader of the first English Baptist church, pleader for liberty of conscience)
etymology: English surname Murton, a variant of Moorton, the settlement on the moor.
biblical_def: John Murton was a furrier of Gainsborough who went into exile with John Smyth's congregation, returned to Spitalfields with Thomas Helwys in 1612, and on Helwys's death led the first English Baptist church. Like Helwys he was imprisoned, and from prison he issued the tracts that carried the argument for full liberty of conscience further than any Englishman had yet taken it: Objections Answered by way of Dialogue (1615) and A Most Humble Supplication (1620). His case was not a plea for toleration of his own party but a principle: that the magistrate bears the sword for civil offences and has no commission over the soul, so that Jew, Turk, and heretic are to be left to God in matters of faith. Roger Williams, who read him, carried the argument to Rhode Island. Joh 4:24 is the ground, that God “is a Spirit” (Joh 4:24) and must be worshipped in spirit and in truth, which no magistrate can compel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions, and toleration as the allowance of religious opinions by law.
webster_full: CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty, power or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions and affections.

TOLERA'TION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved; allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to those of the established church.
MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.

corruption_summary: From prison he argued that the sword reaches the body and not the soul, and that this holds for everyone.
corruption_paragraphs: Murton's argument rests on a distinction the dictionary holds: the magistrate is ordained of God and bears the sword, but he bears it for the purposes Rom 13:4 names, as “a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4) in the civil order. Faith is not produced by the sword and cannot be. Joh 4:24 requires worship in spirit and in truth, and a compelled profession is neither. 1Ti 2:2 tells the church what to ask of rulers: a quiet and peaceable life in godliness and honesty, not an enforced orthodoxy.

What makes Murton's tracts remarkable is the universality he insisted on. He did not ask liberty for Baptists; he argued that the principle covers every man, including those he believed to be in deadly error, because error is answered by the word and not by the gaol. The dictionary names the corruption he was fighting: the use of civil penalties to settle doctrinal questions, by whichever party holds the magistrate's ear. Act 5:29 governs the subject's side of the boundary, and Rom 13:4 the ruler's; Murton's achievement was to state both at once from inside a prison.

pos: n. (Leonard Busher, fl. 1614, English Baptist of Amsterdam, author of Religions Peace, the earliest printed English plea for liberty of conscience)
etymology: English surname Busher, a variant of Bussher, a dweller by the bushes; Leonard, lion-strong.
biblical_def: Leonard Busher describes himself as a citizen of London living in Amsterdam, and almost nothing else about him is certain. What survives is the tract: Religions Peace: or A Plea for Liberty of Conscience, addressed to King James and Parliament and printed in 1614, the earliest known English publication demanding full liberty of conscience in religion. Busher argued that faith is the gift of God and cannot be commanded by statute, that the apostles converted men by preaching and not by prisons, that the forcing of conscience fills the church with hypocrites, and that heretics are to be met with the word. He proposed in plain terms that any man be allowed to write, dispute, or print on religion, provided he kept the civil peace. Isa 55:11 is the confidence the whole plea rests on, that God's word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) and therefore needs no sword.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberty as freedom from restraint, and persecution as the infliction of pain or death for adherence to a particular creed.
webster_full: LIB'ERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense, and applicable to the body, or to the will or mind.
PERSECU'TION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
HYP'OCRITE, n. One who feigns to be what he is not; one who has the form of godliness without the power.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.

corruption_summary: A London exile printed the first English demand for full liberty of conscience and then vanished from the record.
corruption_paragraphs: Busher's central observation is one that persecuting establishments never make about themselves: compulsion does not produce faith, it produces conformity, and a church filled with conformists has been weakened rather than strengthened by the law that filled it. Joh 4:24 requires worship in spirit and in truth, and the state can secure neither. Mat 20:25 describes the exercise of dominion as the way of the princes of the Gentiles, and Mat 20:26 says it shall not be so among Christ's servants.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the confidence underneath the plea. Busher was not an indifferentist; he held the gospel to be true and believed that truth does not require protection by penalty, because Isa 55:11 promises that the word accomplishes what God pleases. The modern mistake runs the other way: liberty of conscience is now commonly argued from the premise that religious claims are not the kind of thing that can be true. Busher argued it from the premise that his were, and that is the only form of the argument a church can honestly make.
